extracted.intended_audience: educators, teachers, and educational theorists interested in training thinking and curriculum design
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and criteria for educating and training children's thinking, including play/work organization, constructive occupations, social learning, and the role of language as a tool of thought. Emphasizes methods that cultivate experimental, reflective, and organized mental habits rather than rote imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use familiar/general cases to interpret rare phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: To be able to substitute the common and frequent fact for that which is relatively rare and peculiar is to reduce the seemingly novel and exceptional to cases of a general and familiar principle, and thus to bring them under control for interpretation and prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explaining unusual events by relating them to well-known principles (example: treat heat as motion because motion is far better experienced); this facilitates interpretation and prediction by anchoring novelty in familiar patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method: produce cases rather than only wait
rubrics_metrics.description: The empirical method says, 'Wait till there is a sufficient number of cases;' the experimental method says, 'Produce the cases.' The latter deliberately and intentionally endeavors to bring about the conjunction (of circumstances). By this method the notion of progress secures scientific warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor deliberate experiment and the intentional production of instances to test hypotheses over passive accumulation of occurrences; use controlled fabrication of cases as an educational method to secure scientific warrant and encourage progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate immediate sensory salience to long-run importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary experience is controlled largely by the direct strength and intensity of various occurrences... Thinking demands the subordination of the immediate stimulus to the remote and distant. The feeble and the minute may be of much greater importance than the glaring and the big.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train students to look beyond bright, loud, or sudden stimuli and to attend to subtle, continuous, or small factors that may indicate important processes; avoid letting conspicuous stimuli monopolize attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate abstraction: deliberate turning away from habitual responses
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain power of abstraction, of deliberate turning away from the habitual responses to a situation, was required before men could be emancipated to follow up suggestions that in the end are fruitful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage deliberate abstraction as a habit—teaching learners to set aside immediate, habitual responses so they can pursue fruitful, less obvious suggestions and general principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience is inclusive and educative when reflective and growing
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience may be interpreted either with reference to the empirical or the experimental attitude of mind. Experience is not a rigid and closed thing; it is vital, and hence growing... The business of education might be defined as just such an emancipation and enlargement of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design education to expand and emancipate experience (not merely record past events): foster reflective experiences that grow intellectual capacity, preserving the child's naive, experimental attitude while guiding its development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of the body as an intellectual problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The child has to learn to do almost everything... These operations of conscious selection and arrangement constitute thinking, though of a rudimentary type... Since mastery of the bodily organs is necessary for all later developments, such problems are both interesting and important, and solving them supplies a very genuine training of thinking power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use activities that require coordination and deliberate selection (reaching, balancing, manipulating) as early intellectual training; treat physical mastery tasks as opportunities to develop conscious selection and arrangement skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social adjustment and speech as engines of intellectual growth
rubrics_metrics.description: In connection with parents, nurse, brother, and sister, the child learns the signs of satisfaction... Speech, the accurate adaptation of sounds heard to the movements of tongue and lips, is, however, the great instrument of social adaptation; and with the development of speech... adaptation of the baby's activities to and with those of other persons gives the keynote of mental life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage social interactions and language development as primary stimuli for extending the child's intellectual range; provide rich social models and communicative contexts that present higher-order problems and meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject naïve imitation as explanation—emphasize attention, selection, experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A child rarely learns by conscious imitation... The word, the gesture, the act, the occupation of another, falls in line with some impulse already active and suggests some satisfactory mode of expression... He selects some of the means he observes, tries them on, finds them successful or unsuccessful... Only because this method is employed is there intellectual discipline and an educative result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pedagogies that assume imitation suffices; teach children to observe critically, select means, experiment, and confirm by results so that imitation becomes a by-product of active problem solving rather than the primary mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use play to build representative capacity and organized ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When things become signs, when they gain a representative capacity as standing for other things, play is transformed from mere physical exuberance into an activity involving a mental factor... In manipulating them, they are living not with the physical things, but in the large world of meanings... Moreover... meanings thus become familiar acquaintances, but they are organized, arranged in groups, made to cohere in connected ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage play that treats objects as signs (part for whole, role-play) to develop concepts, organization of ideas, narrative structure (beginning, middle, end), and coherent mental groupings; value play as formative intellectual work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster playfulness (attitude) rather than mere toy-play (behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Playfulness is a more important consideration than play. The former is an attitude of mind; the latter is a passing outward manifestation of this attitude... The playful attitude is one of freedom. The person is not bound to the physical traits of things...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a playful, imaginative attitude—freedom to treat objects as vehicles of suggestion—while guiding it into meaningful, educative directions; don't mistake mere physical activity for true playfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop work-attitude: interest in adequate embodiment of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Work (as a mental attitude, not as mere external performance) means interest in the adequate embodiment of a meaning in objective form through the use of appropriate materials and appliances... Work means interest in an activity as tending to a culmination, to an outcome, and therefore possessing a thread of continuity binding together its successive stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach continuity of purpose, goal-directed activity, and concern for fitting means to ends; transition children from free play to activities where meaning must find appropriate embodiment and outcomes are anticipated and organized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a sharp, artificial separation between play and work in schooling
rubrics_metrics.description: The sharp break that unfortunately prevails between the kindergarten and the grades is evidence that the theoretical distinction has practical implications... Under the title of play... and under the antithetical caption of work the latter contains many tasks externally assigned... There comes a time when children must extend and make more exact their acquaintance with existing things... Unless these factors are gradually introduced in the earlier play period, they must be introduced later abruptly and arbitrarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design curricula so that play naturally evolves into structured work; introduce goal-directed skills and technical competencies gradually during play periods to avoid abrupt, externally imposed tasks later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not oppose imagination to utility—practical tasks can be educative
rubrics_metrics.description: Activity that is directed upon matters of home and neighborhood interest is depreciated as merely utilitarian... The healthy imagination deals not with the unreal, but with the mental realization of what is suggested... To engage in [homely activities] is to exercise the imagination in constructing an experience of wider value than any the child has yet mastered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include useful, practical activities (cooking, planting, building) as legitimate educational means that can exercise imagination and afford rich, meaningful experience; reject the false dichotomy that practical work stifles imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize constructive occupations to form intellectual habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Manual subjects... may be used for presenting typical problems to be solved by personal reflection and experimentation, and by acquiring definite bodies of knowledge leading later to more specialized scientific knowledge... intelligent consecutive work in gardening, cooking, or weaving... will inevitably result in students amassing information and becoming versed in methods of experimental inquiry and proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan manual and constructive activities so they pose typical problems, require reflection and experimentation, and connect with systematic scientific knowledge; avoid teaching these subjects by rote or external dictation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reorganize curriculum to exploit arts, crafts, and occupations intellectually
rubrics_metrics.description: The only alternative to a reactionary return to the educational traditions of the past lies in working out the intellectual possibilities resident in the various arts, crafts, and occupations, and reorganizing the curriculum accordingly. Here... are found the means by which the blind and routine experience of the race may be transformed into illuminated and emancipated experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate arts, crafts, and occupations into the central curriculum as vehicles for intellectual development and experimental inquiry rather than marginal 'handwork' subjects; reduce overload by making these subjects intellectually productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (signs) is necessary as a tool of thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: While language is not thought it is necessary for thinking as well as for its communication... language includes much more than oral and written speech. Gestures, pictures... anything consciously employed as a sign is, logically, language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat language broadly (including gestures, images, symbols) as indispensable to thinking; use signs intentionally to make meanings accessible, transportable, and manipulable in instructional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use signs to select, preserve, and transfer meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: A verbal sign (a) selects, detaches, a meaning from what is otherwise a vague flux and blur; (b) it retains, registers, stores that meaning; and (c) applies it, when needed, to the comprehension of other things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach naming/labeling to crystallize vague ideas, use language to store meanings for future use, and practice transferring labeled meanings to new contexts to build judgment and inference skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer artificial/intentionally created signs to natural signs for thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural signs are limited... Artificial signs overcome these restrictions. (i) The direct and sensible value of faint sounds and minute written or printed marks is very slight... (ii) Their production is under our direct control... (iii) Arbitrary linguistic signs are convenient and easy to manage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on intentionally designed linguistic and symbolic signs (spoken words, written marks) in teaching to avoid distraction by physical features of natural signs, to permit deliberate use when needed, and to enable compact, portable representation of meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop grammar and language to organize logical classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs not only mark off specific... meanings, but they are also instruments of grouping meanings in relation to one another... Propositions, sentences, bear the same relation to judgments... As is often said, grammar expresses the unconscious logic of the popular mind. The chief intellectual classifications that constitute the working capital of thought have been built up for us by our mother tongue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach language structure and sentence formation to help learners form logical connections, classifications, and conceptual groupings; use linguistic analysis to make implicit logical relations explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not follow 'teach things, not words' literally—teach meanings via language
rubrics_metrics.description: Taken literally, the maxim, 'Teach things, not words,' or 'Teach things before words,' would be the negation of education; it would reduce mental life to mere physical and sensible adjustments. Learning, in the proper sense, is not learning things, but the meanings of things, and this process involves the use of signs, or language in its generic sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pedagogical injunctions that separate words from meanings; use language deliberately to fix and convey meanings—teaching words in conjunction with conceptual understanding rather than as superficial labels or as separable from thought.
